entries.c4f6ce229bbb00c1de67fc47bf99370750e278cb: <div sID="gen11389" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="54" osisID="Ps.54" sID="Ps.54"/> <div eID="gen11389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11390" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11391" type="x-p"/> The key of this psalm hangs at the door, for the title tells us upon what occasion it was penned—when the inhabitants of Ziph, men of Judah (types of Judas the traitor), betrayed David to Saul, by informing him where he was and putting him in a way how to seize him. This they did twice (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19">1 Sam. xxiii. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.1">xxvi. 1</reference>), and it is upon record to their everlasting infamy. The psalm is sweet; the former part of it, perhaps, was meditated when he was in his distress and put into writing when the danger was over, with the addition of the last two verses, which express his thankfulness for the deliverance, which yet might be written in faith, even when he was in the midst of his fright. Here, I. He complains to God of the malice of his enemies, and prays for help against them, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.1-Ps.55.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. He comforts himself with an assurance of the divine favour and protection, and that, in due time, his enemies should be confounded and be delivered, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.4-Ps.55.7">ver. 4-7</reference>. What time we are in distress we may comfortably sing this psalm.
entries.9cfd1fec34f81ecec0912fa24c9516024358df43: <div eID="gen11391" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11390" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Complaints.</title> <div sID="gen11392" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Save me, O God, by thy name, and judge me by thy strength. <hi type="super">2</hi> Hear my prayer, O God; give ear to the words of my mouth. <hi type="super">3</hi> For strangers are risen up against me, and oppressors seek after my soul: they have not set God before them. Selah. <div eID="gen11392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11393" type="x-p"/> We may observe here, 1. The great distress that David was now in, which the title gives an account of. The Ziphim came of their own accord, and informed Saul where David was, with a promise to deliver him into his hand. One would have thought that when David had retired into the country he would not be pursued, into a desert country he would not be discovered, and into his own country he would not be betrayed; and yet it seems he was. Never let a good man expect to be safe an easy till he comes to heaven. How treacherous, how officious, were these Ziphim! It is well that God is faithful, for men are not to be trusted, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.5">Mic. vii. 5</reference>. 2. His prayer to God for succour and deliverance, <reference osisRef="Ps.54.1-Ps.54.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. He appeals to God's strength, by which he was able to help him, and to his name, by which he was engaged to help him, and begs he would save him from his enemies and judge him, that is, plead his cause and judge for him. David has no other plea to depend upon than God's name, no other power to depend upon than God's strength, and those he makes his refuge and confidence. This would be the effectual answer of his prayers (<reference osisRef="Ps.54.2">v. 2</reference>), which even in his flight, when he had not opportunity for solemn address to God, he was ever and anon lifting up to heaven: <hi type="italic">Hear my prayer,</hi> which comes from my heart, and <hi type="italic">give ear to the words of my mouth.</hi> 3. His plea, which is taken from the character of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.54.3">v. 3</reference>. (1.) They are <hi type="italic">strangers;</hi> such were the Ziphites, unworthy the name of Israelites. "They have used me more basely and barbarously than the Philistines themselves would have done." The worst treatment may be expected from those who, having broken through the bonds of relation and alliance, make themselves strangers. (2.) They are <hi type="italic">oppressors;</hi> such was Saul, who, as a king, should have used his power for the protection of all his good subjects, but abused it for their destruction. Nothing is so grievous as oppression in <hi type="italic">the seat of judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Eccl. iii. 16</reference>. Paul's greatest perils were by his <hi type="italic">own countrymen</hi> and by <hi type="italic">false brethren</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.26">2 Cor. xi. 26</reference>), and so were David's. (3.) They were very formidable and threatening; they not only hated him and wished him ill, but they rose up against him in a body, joining their power to do him a mischief. (4.) They were very spiteful and malicious: <hi type="italic">They seek after my soul;</hi> they hunt for the precious life; no less will satisfy them. We may, in faith, pray that God would not by his providence give success, lest it should look like giving countenance, to such cruel bloody men. (5.) They were very profane and atheistical, and, for this reason, he thought God was concerned in honour to appear against them: <hi type="italic">They have not set God before them,</hi> that is, they have quite cast off the thoughts of God; they do not consider that his eye is upon them, that, in fighting against his people, they fight against him, nor have they any dread of the certain fatal consequences of such an unequal engagement. Note, From those who do not set God before them no good is to be expected; nay, what wickedness will not such men be guilty of? What bonds of nature, or friendship, or gratitude, or covenant, will hold those that have broken through the fear of God? <hi type="italic">Selah—Mark this.</hi> Let us all be sure to set God before us at all times; for, if we do not we are in danger of becoming desperate.
entries.5731043c08d8d9e9d2faca603b47c25a42a11b01: <div eID="gen11393" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Consolations.</title> <div sID="gen11394" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Behold, God <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine helper: the Lord <hi type="italic">is</hi> with them that uphold my soul. <hi type="super">5</hi> He shall reward evil unto mine enemies: cut them off in thy truth. <hi type="super">6</hi> I will freely sacrifice unto thee: I will praise thy name, O <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; for <hi type="italic">it is</hi> good. <hi type="super">7</hi> For he hath delivered me out of all trouble: and mine eye hath seen <hi type="italic">his desire</hi> upon mine enemies. <div eID="gen11394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11395" type="x-p"/> We have here the lively actings of David's faith in his prayer, by which he was assured that the issue would be comfortable, though the attempt upon him was formidable. <div eID="gen11395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11396" type="x-p"/> I. He was sure that he had God on his side, that God took his part (<reference osisRef="Ps.54.4">v. 4</reference>); he speaks it with an air of triumph and exultation, <hi type="italic">Behold, God is my helper.</hi> If we be for him, he is for us; and, if he be for us, we shall have such help in him that we need not fear any power engaged against us. Though men and devils aim to be our destroyers, they shall not prevail while God is our helper: <hi type="italic">The Lord is with those that uphold my soul.</hi> Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.118.7">Ps. cxviii. 7</reference>, "<hi type="italic">The Lord taketh my part with those that help me.</hi> There are some that uphold me, and God is one of them; he is the principal one; none of them could help me if he did not help them." Every creature is that to us (and no more) that God makes it to be. He means, "The Lord is he that upholds my soul, and keeps me from tiring in my work and sinking under my burdens." He that by his providence upholds all things by his grace upholds the souls of his people. God, who will in due time save his people, does, in the mean time, sustain them and bear them up, so that the spirit he has made shall not fail before him. <div eID="gen11396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11397" type="x-p"/> II. God taking part with him, he doubted not but his enemies should both flee and fall before him (<reference osisRef="Ps.54.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He shall reward evil unto my enemies that observe me,</hi> seeking an opportunity to do me a mischief. The evil they designed against me the righteous God will return upon their own heads." David would not render evil to them, but he knew God would: <hi type="italic">I as a deaf man heard not, for thou wilt hear.</hi> The enemies we forgive, if they repent not, God will judge; and for this reason we must not avenge ourselves, because God has said, <hi type="italic">Vengeance is mine.</hi> But he prays, <hi type="italic">Cut them off in thy truth.</hi> This is not a prayer of malice, but a prayer of faith; for it has an eye to the word of God, and only desires the performance of that. There is truth in God's threatenings as well as in his promises, and sinners that repent not will find it so to their cost. <div eID="gen11397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11398" type="x-p"/> III. He promises to give thanks to God for all the experiences he had had of his goodness to him (<reference osisRef="Ps.54.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will sacrifice unto thee.</hi> Though sacrifices were expensive, yet, when God required that his worshippers should in that way praise him, David would not only offer them, but offer them freely and without grudging. All our spiritual sacrifices must, in this sense, be free-will-offerings; for God loves a cheerful giver. Yet he will not only bring his sacrifice, which was but the shadow, the ceremony; he will mind the substance: <hi type="italic">I will praise thy name.</hi> A thankful heart, and the calves of our lips giving thanks to his name, are the sacrifices God will accept: "<hi type="italic">I will praise thy name, for it is good.</hi> Thy name is not only great but good, and therefore to be praised. To praise thy name is not only what we are bound to, but it is good, it is pleasant, it is profitable; it is good for us (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.1">Ps. xcii. 1</reference>); therefore <hi type="italic">I will praise thy name.</hi>" <div eID="gen11398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11399" type="x-p"/> IV. He speaks of his deliverance as a thing done (<reference osisRef="Ps.54.7">v. 7</reference>): I will praise thy name, and say, "<hi type="italic">He has delivered me;</hi> this shall be my song then." That which he rejoices in is a complete deliverance—<hi type="italic">He has delivered me from all trouble;</hi> and a deliverance to his heart's content—<hi type="italic">My eye has seen its desire upon my enemies,</hi> not seen them cut off and ruined, but forced to retreat, tidings being brought to Saul that the Philistines were upon him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.27-1Sam.23.28">1 Sam. xxiii. 27, 28</reference>. All David desired was to be himself safe; when he saw Saul draw off his forces he saw his desire. <hi type="italic">He has delivered me from all trouble.</hi> Either, 1. With this thought David comforted himself when he was in distress: "<hi type="italic">He has delivered me from all trouble</hi> hitherto, and many a time I have gained my point, and seen my desire on my enemies; therefore he will deliver me out of this trouble." We should thus, in our greatest straits, encourage ourselves with our past experiences. Or, 2. With this thought he magnified his present deliverance when the fright was over, that it was an earnest of further deliverance. He speaks of the completing of his deliverance as a thing done, though he had as yet many troubles before him, because, having God's promise for it, he was as sure of it as if it had been done already. "He that has begun to deliver me from all troubles, and will at length give me to see my desire upon my enemies." This may perhaps point at Christ, of whom David was a type; God would deliver him out of all the troubles of his state of humiliation, and he was perfectly sure of it; and all things are said to be put under his feet; for, though we see not yet all things put under him, yet we are sure he shall reign till all his enemies be made his footstool, and he shall see his desire upon them. However, it is an encouragement to all believers to make that use of their particular deliverances which St. Paul does (like David here), <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17-2Tim.4.18">2 Tim. iv. 17, 18</reference>, <hi type="italic">He that delivered me from the mouth of the lion shall deliver me from every evil work, and will preserve me to his heavenly kingdom.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.54"/> <div eID="gen11399" type="x-p"/>

See on <reference osisRef="Ps.4.1">Psa 4:1</reference>, title; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1">Psa 32:1</reference>, title; for the history, see <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19">1Sa 23:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.29">29</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.1-1Sam.26.25">26:1-25</reference>. After an earnest cry for help, the Psalmist promises praise in the assurance of a hearing.</title> <div sID="gen9288" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6080"/><hi type="bold">1. by thy name--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.5.11">Psa 5:11</reference>), specially, power.<div eID="gen9288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9289" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judge me--</hi>as in <reference osisRef="Ps.7.8">Psa 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.26.1">26:1</reference>. <div eID="gen9289" type="x-p"/>

(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.4.1">Psa 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.5.1">5:1</reference>). <div eID="gen9290" type="x-p"/>
entries.13fbcdda727ad0d48c83cea243a6f7be1f5441b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6082"/><div sID="gen9291" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6082"/><hi type="bold">3. strangers--</hi>perhaps Ziphites.<div eID="gen9291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9292" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oppressors--</hi>literally, "terrible ones" (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">Is 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.3">25:3</reference>). Such were Saul and his army.<div eID="gen9292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9293" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not set ... them--</hi>acted as atheists, without God's fear (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.16.8">Psa 16:8</reference>). <div eID="gen9293" type="x-p"/>
entries.80f2a0a946bfd343c167a7d551ccfd4fdf559fcf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6083"/><div sID="gen9294" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6083"/>4. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.30.10">Psa 30:10</reference>).<div eID="gen9294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9295" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with them--</hi>on their side, and for me (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.46.11">Psa 46:11</reference>). <div eID="gen9295" type="x-p"/>
entries.c507c354c098a0e8ec0a0c591fa5d7b75d9df643: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6084"/><div sID="gen9296" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6084"/><hi type="bold">5. He shall ... evil--</hi>or, "Evil shall return on" (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.16">Psa 7:16</reference>) my enemies or watchers, that is, to do me evil (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.7">Psa 6:7</reference>).<div eID="gen9296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9297" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in thy truth--</hi>Thy verified promise. <div eID="gen9297" type="x-p"/>
entries.6be2920e85c3ee60eb6e4c0ed4ae72203224b9db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6085"/><div sID="gen9298" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6085"/><hi type="bold">6. entries.4e4bfe47011795eb1af9411bdf2ddc58064fe75d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6086"/><div sID="gen9299" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6086"/><hi type="bold">7. mine eye ... desire--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Ps.59.10">Psa 59:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.112.8">112:8</reference>), expresses satisfaction in beholding the overthrow of his enemies as those of God, without implying any selfish or unholy feeling (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.52.6">Psa 52:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.52.7">7</reference>). <chapter eID="Ps.54"/>

entries.9edddfb42d6a7d18bbf3e38e1b06695bb16f587d: <div eID="gen20326" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20327" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20328" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20328" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20327" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20329" type="x-p"/> The psalmist complains that strangers were risen up against him to take away his life, <reference osisRef="Psa.54.1-Psa.54.3">Psa 54:1-3</reference>; expresses his confidence in God that he will uphold him, and punish his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.54.4">Psa 54:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.54.5">Psa 54:5</reference>; on which he promises to sacrifice to God, <reference osisRef="Psa.54.6">Psa 54:6</reference>; he speaks of his deliverance, <reference osisRef="Psa.54.7">Psa 54:7</reference>. <div eID="gen20329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20330" type="x-p"/> The title is, "To the chief Musician upon Neginoth, an instructive Psalm of David, when the Ziphites came to Saul, and said, Doth not David conceal himself among us?" <div eID="gen20330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20331" type="x-p"/> Ziph was a village in the southern part of Palestine. David having taken refuge in the mountains of that country, the Ziphites went to Saul, and informed him of the fact. Saul, with his army, immediately went thither, and was on one side of a mountain while David was on the other. Just when he was about to fall into the hands of his merciless pursuer, an express came to Saul that the Philistines had invaded Israel, on which he gave up the pursuit, and returned to save his country, and David escaped to En-gedi. See the account in <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19-1Sam.23.29">1Sam 23:19-29</reference>. It is supposed to have been after this deliverance that he composed this Psalm. Neginoth, from נגן nagan to strike or play on some kind of instrument, probably signifies stringed instruments, such as were played on with a plectrum. <div eID="gen20331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20332" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20333" type="x-p"/> Save me, O God, by thy name - Save me by thyself alone; so name here may be understood. The name of God is often God himself. David was now in such imminent danger of being taken and destroyed, that no human means were left for his escape; if God therefore had not Interfered, he must have been destroyed. See the introduction, <reference osisRef="Psa.54.1-Psa.54.7">Psa 54:1-7</reference> (note).
entries.ea8cfe9df8346d2e2095abc2b92612050425a0e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20334" type="x-p"/> Hear my prayer - In his straits he had recourse to God; for from him alone, for the reasons alleged above, his deliverance must proceed.
entries.2972fcba65a0e4a35c32c7783818c3bd71bb4ada: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20335" type="x-p"/> Strangers are risen up against me - The Ziphites. <div eID="gen20335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20336" type="x-p"/> And oppressors - Saul, his courtiers, and his army. <div eID="gen20336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20337" type="x-p"/> They have not set God before them - It is on no religious account, nor is it to accomplish any end, on which they can ask the blessing of God. <div eID="gen20337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20338" type="x-p"/> Selah - This is true.
entries.af41be90f05fcf95fcbf37448bb3e195870b8510: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20339" type="x-p"/> Behold, God is mine helper - This would naturally occur to him when he saw that Saul was obliged to leave the pursuit, and go to defend his territories, when he was on the very point of seizing him. God, whose providence is ever watchful, had foreseen this danger and stirred up the Philistines to make this inroad just at the time in which Saul and his army were about to lay hands on David. Well might he then say, "Behold, God is mine helper." <div eID="gen20339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20340" type="x-p"/> Is with them, that uphold my soul - נפשי naphshi, my life. This may even refer to the Philistines, who had at this time made an inroad on Israel. God was even with his own enemies, by making them instruments to save the life of his servant.
entries.0c65816de5ac01d0a8f324117670c62dd26b1f0b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20341" type="x-p"/> He shall reward evil - Saul and his courtiers, instead of having God's approbation, shall have his curse. <div eID="gen20341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20342" type="x-p"/> Cut them off in thy truth - Thou hast promised to save me; these have purposed to destroy me. Thy truth is engaged in my defence; they will destroy me if permitted to live: to save thy truth, and to accomplish its promises, thou must cut them off.
entries.9a792bd4011596584f536a48ed69c35b6644420f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20343" type="x-p"/> I will freely sacrifice unto thee - Or, I will sacrifice nobly unto thee. Not only with a willing mind, but with a liberal hand will I bring sacrifice unto thee. <div eID="gen20343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20344" type="x-p"/> For it is good - Thy name is good; it is descriptive of thy nature; full of goodness and mercy to man. And it is good to be employed in such a work: whoever worships thee in sincerity is sure to be a gainer. To him who orders his conversation aright, thou dost show thy salvation.
entries.b3d87f8fd1bc749f2a34df325d5625ea0b3e4daf: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20345" type="x-p"/> For he hath delivered me - Saul had now decamped; and was returned to save his territories; and David in the meanwhile escaped to En-gedi. God was most evidently the author of this deliverance. <div eID="gen20345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20346" type="x-p"/> Mine eye hath seen his desire upon mine enemies - It is not likely that this Psalm was written after the death of Saul; and therefore David could not say that he had seen his desire. But there is nothing in the text for his desire; and the words might be translated, My eye hath seen my enemies - they have been so near that I could plainly discover them. Thus almost all the Versions have understood the text. I have seen them, and yet they were not permitted to approach me. God has been my Deliverer.  <chapter eID="Ps.54"/> <div eID="gen20346" type="x-p"/>

entries.a8bfee0254847356f7f1449731e698b2f0f5ab9b: <reference osisRef="Ps.54.1-Ps.54.3">Psa 54:1-3</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_54:3-5) This short song is divided into two parts by <hi type="italic">Sela</hi> The first half prays for help and answer. The Name of God is the manifestation of His nature, which has mercy as its central point (for the Name of God is טּוב, v. 8, Ps 52:11), so that בּשׁמך (which is here the parallel word to בּגבוּרתך) is consequently equivalent to בּחסדּך. The obtaining of right for any one (דּין like שׁפט, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.9">Psa 7:9</reference>, and frequently, עשׂה דּין, <reference osisRef="Ps.9.5">Psa 9:5</reference>) is attributed to the all-conquering might of God, which is only one side of the divine Name, i.e., of the divine nature which manifests itself in the diversity of its attributes. האזין (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.54.4">Psa 54:4</reference></hi>) is construed with ל (cf. אל, <reference osisRef="Ps.87.2">Psa 87:2</reference>) like הטּה אזן, Psa 78:1. The Targum, misled by <reference osisRef="Ps.86.14">Psa 86:14</reference>, reads זרים instead of זרים in Psa 54:5. The inscription leads one to think of the Ziphites in particular in connection with “strangers” and “violent men.” The two words in most instances denote foreign enemies, Isa 25:2., <reference osisRef="Ps.29.5">Psa 29:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.12">Eze 31:12</reference>; but זר is also a stranger in the widest sense, regulated in each instance according to the opposite, e.g., the non-priest, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.10">Lev 22:10</reference>; and one’s fellow-countrymen can also turn out to be עריצים, Jer 15:21. The Ziphites, although Judaeans like David, might be called “strangers,” because they had taken the side against David; and “violent men,” because they pledged themselves to seize and deliver him up. Under other circumstances this might have been their duty as subjects. In this instance, however, it was godlessness, as <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.54.5">Psa 54:5</reference></hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.86.14">Psa 86:14</reference>) says. Any one at that time in Israel who feared God more than man, could not lend himself to be made a tool of Saul’s blind fury. God had already manifestly enough acknowledged David.
entries.85a0c3546b294fc7a7d7b9956c6542be1040a0ae: <reference osisRef="Ps.54.4-Ps.54.7">Psa 54:4-7</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_54:6-9) In this second half, the poet, in the certainty of being heard, rejoices in help, and makes a vow of thanksgiving. The בּ of בּסמכי is not meant to imply that God is one out of many who upheld his threatened life; but rather that He comes within the category of such, and fills it up in Himself alone, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.118.7">Psa 118:7</reference>; and for the origin of this <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> <hi type="italic">essentiae</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.99.6">Psa 99:6</reference>, Jdg 11:35. In <reference osisRef="Ps.54.7">Psa 54:7</reference> the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> merits the preference over the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> (evil shall “revert” to my spies), which would at least require על instead of ל (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.7.17">Psa 7:17</reference>). Concerning שׁררי, vid., on Psa 27:11. In the rapid transition to invocation in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.54.7">Psa 54:7</reference></hi> the end of the Psalm announces itself. The truth of God is not described as an instrumental agent of the cutting off, but as an impelling cause. It is the same <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> as in the expression בּנדבה (Num 15:3): by or out of free impulse. These free-will sacrifices are not spiritual here in opposition to the ritual sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.14">Psa 50:14</reference>), but ritual as an outward representation of the spiritual. The subject of הצּילני is the Name of God; the post-biblical language, following <reference osisRef="Lev.24.11">Lev 24:11</reference>, calls God straightway השּׁם, and passages like <reference osisRef="Isa.30.27">Isa 30:27</reference> and the one before us come very near to this usage. The praeterites mention the ground of the thanksgiving. What David now still hopes for will then lie behind him in the past. The closing line, v. 9 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, recalls <reference osisRef="Ps.35.21">Psa 35:21</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.59.11">Psa 59:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.92.12">Psa 92:12</reference>; the invoking of the curse upon his enemies in v. 8 recalls <reference osisRef="Ps.17.13">Psa 17:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.56.8">Psa 56:8</reference>; Psa 59:12.; and the vow of thanksgiving in v. 8 recalls <reference osisRef="Ps.22.26">Psa 22:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.18">Psa 35:18</reference>; Psa 40:10.  <chapter eID="Ps.54"/> <div eID="gen9551" type="x-p"/>

entries.06736f018d6053de3ca2275909040e31265b174b:
PSALM 54
David has recorded in this psalm the prayers which he offered up to God when he heard of his having been betrayed by the Ziphites, and was reduced to a situation of extreme danger. It cannot fail to impress us with a high idea of his indomitable faith, thus to find him calling upon the name of God in the immediate prospect of death.
To the chief musician on Neginoth. A Psalm of David for instruction: when the Ziphites came and said to Saul, Doth not David hide himself with us?
We know from the sacred history that David frequently concealed himself in that part of the wilderness which adjoined to the Ziphites. It appears (1 Samuel 23:19; 26:1) that he was betrayed by them on two different occasions; and he takes notice of the particular circumstances in which the psalm was written, to teach us that we should never despair of divine help even in the worst situation. Surrounded as he was by hostile troops, and hemmed in on every side by apparently inevitable destruction, we cannot but admire the rare and heroical intrepidity which he displayed in committing himself, by prayer, to the Almighty. It might have appeared just as credible that God could bring the dead out of the grave, as that he could preserve him in such circumstances; for it seemed impossible that he should escape from the cave where he was concealed with his life.
Psalm 54:1-3
1. Save me, O God! by thy name, and judge me by thy strength. 2. Hear my prayer, O God! give ear to the words of my mouth. 3. For strangers are risen up against me, and the terrible ones have sought after my soul they have not set God before them. Selah.
 
1. Save me, O God! As David was at this time placed beyond the reach of human assistance, he must be understood as praying to be saved by the name and the power of God, In an emphatical sense, or by these in contradistinction to the usual means of deliverance. Though all help must ultimately come from God, there are ordinary methods by which he generally extends it. When these fail, and every earthly stay is removed, he must then take the work into his own hands. It was in such a situation that David here fled to the saints’ last asylum, and sought to be saved by a miracle of divine power. By appealing, in the second part of the verse, to God as his judge, he asserts his uprightness. And it must strike us all, that in asking the divine protection it is indispensably prerequisite we should be convinced of the goodness of our cause, as it would argue the greatest profanity in any to expect that God should patronise iniquity. David was encouraged to pray for deliverance by the goodness of his cause and his consciousness of integrity; nor did he entertain a single doubt, that on representing this to God he would act the part of his defender, and punish the cruelty and treachery of his enemies.
